texts.text: In most circumstances, guidelines will permit the ambulance crews to assess patient
condition/chief complaint and initiate the appropriate levels of care.
It should be understood that when a crew is in doubt concerning a patient's condition,
or the appropriate care to be initiated, the paramedic should never hesitate to contact
medical control for any problem, question or for additional orders.
Verbally repeat all orders received from medical control prior to initiation of these orders.
Patients with significant injuries/illness that require immediate intervention should be
transported promptly avoiding extended scene times. Patient care interventions should be
initiated in route as often as possible with major traumas, critical medical conditions.
Any patient with diabetic history with signs/symptoms of hypoglycemia should be
assessed on scene, and ALS interventions should be initiated during transport. Due to
underlying medical conditions/pathologies, unless it is absolutely necessary to initiate
ALS interventions on scene, crews should transport patients to the appropriate medical
facilities without delays. Should it be necessary to initiate care on scene (patient with
decreased LOC but is refusing transport or similar problems) then the paramedic must
clearly document care given, and report will be reviewed by medical director (If patient
was treated but not transported). In most situations it will be expected that patients will
be transported with interventions initiated during transport.
All trauma patients with major, moderate injuries should receive (2) IVs, or IO,
preferably with large bore IV catheters. Trauma patients with signs/symptoms of
hypotension (systolic BP < 90mmhg) should receive IV, and consider fluid challenge
until the systolic BP is at least 90mmhg. (Fluid challenge 20 ml/kg)
Intraosseous access should be initiated after (2) failed IV attempts, or should be
initiated immediately if immediate peripheral access is not available or possible.
All pediatric peripheral IV/IO’s, should be setup with burette set control devices.
Proper endotracheal tube placement must be documented by at least three different
confirmation methods. These include: Presence of bilateral breath sounds, absence of
breath sounds over the epigastrium, waveform capnography, visualizing the tube passing
through the cords; presence of condensation on the inside of the ET tube.
When administering drug via the ET tube, administer 2.0 - 2.5 times the IV dose. Dilute
the drug with NS to result in a total of 10 ml.

these instances, crews must follow established guidelines and should any
controversy occur, initiate contact with medical control and place the on scene

being transported from the physician's office. Even in these circumstances, assuring
guidelines are followed is important. Should the physician differ significantly from
BRMC protocols, advise the physician of our protocols in a professional manner.
